messages.content: i have two things i would like to do tomorrow afternoon. my friend wants to read together, and my sister wants to go for a walk. i have time for only one.
you could first check whether either person has another time free. you may not have to give up one idea if one can happen on another day.
my friend can read with me the next morning. my sister is only free tomorrow afternoon.
then one possible plan is to walk with your sister tomorrow afternoon and read with your friend the next morning, if you have that morning free too.
i do not know if i am free the next morning. i only know my friend is.
then check your own time before saying yes. your friend being free does not make that a time when both of you can meet.
write a short message that does not say yes yet.
i would like to read with you. i need to check whether i am free that morning before we choose it.
can i still say yes to the walk now?
yes, if tomorrow afternoon works for you and you want to go. you can choose the walk while keeping the reading time open.
there is a note in my book saying stop here. does that mean there is no more story after that page?
not always. it could be a note about where someone stopped reading, or a request to leave the next part for later. look at the context before thinking that the whole story is finished there.
give a simple answer.
no. the note might be about where a person stopped reading. it does not have to mean the book has no more story after that page.
write a little story where two friends left that note for reading together.

two friends read a book after school. they reach a part where a girl is about to open a door, but they have to go home. one writes stop here on a card and puts it between the pages. the next day, they find the card and begin from that part. neither friend read the next part alone, so they can learn what is behind the door together.
keep only the last sentence.
neither friend read the next part alone, so they can learn what is behind the door together.
why did they use a card?
the card helped them find their place without writing the note on the book page.
tell me a story where a mother helps a child answer a question by looking at what is already there.

a child asks how many cups are on the table. his mother could give the answer, but she asks him to look at the table with her. he sees two near the book and one by the plate. he says there are three. then he sees a picture of a cup in the book and asks whether that is another one. she asks whether someone can drink from the picture. he says no. they keep the answer at three real cups on the table.
ask my request simply.
tell me a story where a mother helps a child answer by looking at the things in front of him.
why did the picture not make four cups?
it was a picture of a cup, rather than a cup someone could use. the question was about the real cups on the table.
what if the question asks how many cups and pictures of cups i can see?
then the picture is part of what the question asks for, and the answer is four. different words in the question can change what you should count.
make that answer simple.
if the question asks for real cups and pictures of cups together, the answer is four.
my brother and i are writing one letter to our aunt. we both want to say thank you, but only i visited her garden.
you can use we for the part you both want to say, then make the garden part about you alone. that keeps the letter from saying your brother was there too.
write a short example without giving either of us a name.
we want to thank you for thinking of us. i also enjoyed visiting your garden and would like to come again.
our aunt did not do something for both of us. my brother just wants to say hello.
then the letter could say: hello from both of us. i enjoyed visiting your garden and wanted to thank you for having me.
can you say my brother wants to visit too?
only if that is true. you have not told me whether he wants to visit. you can ask him before adding that to a letter from both of you.
he says yes. add it clearly.
hello from both of us. i enjoyed visiting your garden and wanted to thank you for having me. my brother would like to visit too.
does a letter from both mean every sentence has to use we?
no. it can have a part about both people and another part about just one, as long as that is clear.
i have a closed container on my desk. i do not remember what is inside. can you tell from that information?
no. being closed and on a desk does not tell me what is inside. looking inside or knowing what you put there would give more information.
answer simply.
no. i do not know what is inside. looking inside or knowing what you put there would give more information.
can you write a made up story where it holds a letter?

a child finds a closed container on a desk. she asks her father whether she can open it. he says yes. inside is a letter from her grandmother, along with a small picture of a garden. they sit together and read the letter before putting it back.
in the real conversation, does your story tell me what my container holds?
no. the story is made up. it does not give information about the real container on your desk.
what question could you ask me instead of making something up?
do you remember the last thing you put in the container?
my friend says either day works when i ask about tomorrow or the day after. does that mean we must meet on both days?
no. either day works says that you can choose one of those days. it does not mean you have to meet on both.
what if i say both days work for me too?
then each of you is free on both days, but you still need to choose whether to meet once or more than once. being free does not make every possible meeting a plan.
write a message choosing tomorrow only.
let us meet tomorrow, then. we can leave the other day open.
now let my friend answer that tomorrow only works after lunch.
tomorrow works after lunch. i am busy in the morning.
make my last request simple.
write a reply saying tomorrow works after lunch, but the morning is busy.
what should i check before saying the plan is ready?
check that after lunch works for you too and choose a place if you have not already done that.
i want a quiet story where nothing is lost and there is no big problem. make it about getting a room ready for reading.

a woman opens the window in a small room. she puts two chairs near the table and brings a book from the shelf. her brother comes in with two cups of tea. they talk for a few minutes, then choose a page to read together. one reads while the other listens. outside, people walk along the street, but the room feels calm. after a while, they close the book and leave the next part for tomorrow.
ask my first request in fewer words.
write a quiet story about getting a room ready for reading.
did they finish the whole book?
no. they kept the next part for tomorrow. they enjoyed some reading without having to finish everything in one visit.
can you give the story a short name?
a room for reading.
choose another name.
tea and a book.
why can a story work without a big problem?
a story can give us a moment, a place, or time with people. a big problem is one way to make a story, but it is not the only way.
i sent my friend a message saying see you at three. later, i found out they had not read it. did that change our plan from two to three?
not by itself. if you had both chosen two before, your new message gave a different time that your friend had not seen. you cannot know that they understood the new time.
say it simply.
if you both chose two before, one new message does not tell us that your friend knows about three. check before thinking you both have the same plan.
what should i ask?
did you see my message about three? does that time work for you?
my friend says they can only come at two. i can do two after all.
then tell them that two still works for you. you do not need to keep three just because you sent a message about it.
write the reply.
two works for me too. let us keep the original time.
what is the plan now?
you are both keeping two as the meeting time. the idea of three was not the plan you both chose.
my daughter likes asking questions while i read to her. sometimes we stop so often that we forget what happened in the story.
you could keep a card for questions. when a question is not needed to understand the next part, write a few words on the card and return to it at a good place to stop.
keep just the part about the card.
write a few words on the card and return to the question at a good place to stop.
what if she needs the answer to understand what happens next?
then stop and talk about that question now. the card is there to help, rather than to keep every question out of the reading.
can you write a short conversation about using the card?

why does the girl leave the village? let us look at that now because it helps with the next page. what color is her house? we can keep that on the card and look back later if the story gives us that detail.
keep just the last sentence.
we can keep that on the card and look back later if the story gives us that detail.
should the child never ask while i read?
no. the idea is to make room for both the story and the questions, not to stop her from asking.
i wrote a story about a person on a train. i want your help, but do not add family or work details for the person.
i can keep those details open. what kind of help do you want with the train part?
i want the person to see something outside that makes them ask a question.
the person looks through the window and sees a small house near a garden. they ask who lives there and how far the house is from town.
make that part simple.
the person sees a small house near a garden and asks who lives there.
did you choose whether the person says the question for someone else to hear?
not clearly. they ask could mean asking someone, but if you want it to be a thought, we should say that. the sentence needs that detail to be clear.
make the thought clear without having the person speak.
the person sees a small house near a garden and thinks about who lives there and how far it is from town.
now keep only the question they have in mind.
who lives in that house, and how far is it from town?
i have a book, a cup, and a small container on the table. are all three objects?
yes. all three are objects. object is a general word for things that can be different from each other.
say it simply.
yes. a book, a cup, and a container are all objects.
keep just yes and the three things.
yes: the book, the cup, and the container.
if i call them objects, can you still know which one i want to read?
not from object alone. book gives the specific kind, while object is general. to keep the difference, you need the more specific word or other context.
what if i say the object with pages?
from the three things you gave, the book is the one with pages. the context helps us choose it.
give the answer with just book and context.
the context helps us choose the book.
i want to read with my brother once this week, but we do not know which day. can we still say we have a plan?
you have a general plan to read together, but the day is still open. you can keep the goal while saying that one detail is not chosen yet.
write a message about that to my mother.
we want to read together once this week. we have not chosen the day yet.
now my brother says he is free tomorrow, but i am not. does that end the idea?
no. it only says that tomorrow does not work for both of you. you can ask about another day instead of giving up the whole idea.
i am free the day after tomorrow. ask him about it.
would the day after tomorrow work for reading together?
he says yes after lunch. write the plan in one sentence.
we will read together after lunch the day after tomorrow.
what detail could still be useful before we meet?
a place to meet and which book to bring would help if you have not chosen those yet.
